title: Thailand's Flood Wrecked the Hard Disk Drive Industry: The Biggest Factory Fell, the Number Two Took the Throne
dek: A flood in Thailand rewrote the hard drive rankings: the largest factory, Western Digital, saw shipments fall 51% quarter-over-quarter, while Seagate fell only 8% and overtook it to take the top spot.
why: What are the risks of geographic concentration in manufacturing supply chains? This flood provides a complete case study—industrial estate siting, zero inventory, and single points of failure can all detonate at once.
who: Production decision-makers preparing to or already building factories in Southeast Asia, investors watching the hard drive and storage industry landscape, and engineers doing supply chain risk management.
skip: The opening history of Thai rivers and dam building can be skipped; start at the 3-minute mark with why the hard drive industry moved to Thailand.

points.h: Flood walls gave hard drive factories a false sense of security
points.body: The industrial estates were built on river floodplains converted from rice paddies north of Bangkok. To prevent flooding, developers installed ring levees up to two meters high, secondary wave walls, pumps, and drainage systems; the estates quickly grew into small cities with their own housing and shops. But this engineering may have misled everyone. When the real flood season arrived in 2011, seven industrial estates were inundated within two weeks. Research later suspected that it was precisely this seemingly complete infrastructure that created a false confidence—the belief that even if it rained, everything would be fine. In other words, what manufacturers bought was not safety, but an illusion of risk.

points.h: Reservoir releases were not the culprit; local rainfall was
points.body: After the flood, dam managers were blamed for releasing water too late, with criticism focusing on favoritism toward farmers and rice corruption allegations. But research does not support this attribution. A 2023 simulation tested 17 scenarios for the release strategies of two dams and concluded that even if operators had perfect foresight of subsequent rainfall, the flooded area could have been reduced by at most only 3.68%. Another 2020 study examined data from hydrological stations along the Chao Phraya River and found that in one low-lying disaster area, less than 30% of the floodwater came from the river, while 73.7% came from local rainfall. In other words, the water mainly fell directly on the disaster area, and reservoir decisions cannot take the blame.

points.h: Why did Seagate, which was not flooded, also stop?
points.body: Seagate's factory in northern Korat was largely unaffected, but production still halted—because seven of its top ten suppliers were flooded. A typical case was Japan's Nidec, which makes spindle motors for hard drives; two of its plants were submerged and production stopped outright. The hard drive supply chain is interlocking layer by layer: no matter how safe the assembly line, if the motor doesn't arrive, the whole line stops. Seagate managed to limit its quarterly shipment decline to 8% by quickly qualifying new suppliers, modifying designs to reduce complexity, and negotiating payment terms with suppliers. In the same year, Western Digital's core factory was flooded to a depth of 1.8 meters, and its quarterly shipments fell 51%. The difference between the two was not whose building was taller, but whose supply chain could more quickly bypass the break point.

points.h: Zero inventory amplified the flood into a global shortage
points.body: Before the flood hit, the hard drive industry had just completed a round of consolidation: Western Digital announced its acquisition of Hitachi's hard drive business in March 2011, and a month later Seagate announced its acquisition of Samsung, barely bringing supply and demand back into balance. Precisely because there was no excess inventory to draw down, the shock was multiplied. Tom Coughlin estimated that in the fourth quarter of 2011, hard drive demand was about 180 million units, while actual production was only 110 million to 120 million units; and the flood happened to hit right in the Christmas shopping season. Retailers immediately raised spot prices by 20% to 40%, and a 1TB hard drive at Taipei's Guanghua Market jumped from NT$1,750 to over NT$3,000. Even Intel admitted in December that Q4 revenue would be about $1 billion less than expected due to the hard drive shortage. A local flood, transmitted through zero inventory, thus became a global shortage.

points.h: The flood receded, but hard drive prices didn't fall for two years
points.body: The water receded, but the shortage did not end quickly. Hard drive supply availability returned to pre-disaster levels only about nine months later; retail prices fell back even more slowly—hard drive prices on Newegg did not drop back to pre-disaster levels until April 2013. Backblaze used its own procurement records to calculate: in September 2011, the cost per GB was $0.044, and it would take until September 2013 to return to that level. Why is it easy to raise prices but hard to lower them? The author lists several interpretations: the ecosystem recovered more slowly than expected, the two giants' 2011 acquisitions brought additional costs, tablet computers caused a permanent decline in PC hard drive demand, and a more cynical guess—after Seagate and Western Digital acquired second-tier rivals, only three major manufacturers remained in the entire industry, making prices easier to "stabilize," or in his own word: cartelize. As for which one is the truth, he does not conclude.

points.h: The flooded giant chose to stay and keep building walls
points.body: Western Digital's post-disaster choice is telling: it did not retreat, but doubled down on defenses. WD and the Bang Pa-in estate owner built an 11-kilometer flood wall along the estate, and WD added a 6-meter-high inner wall around its factory; to add redundancy to its supply chain, in December 2011 it announced a new slider fab in Malaysia. A survey of 50 directly affected Japanese companies showed that nearly 80% decided to stay in Thailand. The reasons are not hard to understand: ready-made estates, supporting facilities, and skilled workers are hard to pack up and take away. Thailand has since suffered multiple rounds of major flooding, especially in the 2020s almost every year; in November of the most recent year, it even rained what was called a "once-in-300-years" storm, but these estates have held out so far. Whether stronger defenses will be needed in the future can only be tested by the next major flood.
